hooks.text: A wasp slips one egg inside a cockroach’s egg case. What happens next turns the roach eggs into food.
hooks.payoff: Explain how the ensign wasp’s egg develops into a larva that feeds on the cockroach eggs inside the case.

hooks.text: A dozen cockroach eggs can feed one baby wasp. How does it get inside their egg case?
hooks.payoff: Reveal that the female ensign wasp places one egg inside the case, putting her developing young among its food.

hooks.text: A cockroach’s egg case can become another insect’s nursery. And the cockroach eggs are on the menu.
hooks.payoff: Reveal that the other insect is an ensign wasp: the female lays an egg inside the cockroach egg case, and the developing larva feeds on the roach eggs.

hooks.text: A cockroach’s egg case can have an extra egg inside. It belongs to a completely different insect.
hooks.payoff: Identify the extra egg as an ensign wasp egg and explain how its larva feeds on the cockroach eggs around it.

hooks.text: This wasp doesn’t sting people. But its babies eat cockroach eggs. How do they get inside?
hooks.payoff: Introduce the ensign wasp, distinguish its harmlessness to people from its larva’s feeding, and explain how the female places an egg inside a cockroach egg case.

editorial_review: Hook 1 opens with the egg placement and leaves the development sequence for narration.
Hook 2 uses the source quote stating a dozen or more eggs as food for the larva; baby wasp is plain language for its young.
Hook 3 uses nursery and menu as metaphors for the larva developing and feeding inside the case.
Hook 4 leaves the identity of the added egg for the next narration beat.
Hook 5 contrasts the adult not stinging people with its young feeding on eggs. It refers to this source species, not all wasps.
No claim of infestation, complete control, universal roach hosts or guaranteed performance.
provenance: Subscription writer output retained separately. Operator tightened hooks 2 through 5 for plain language and curiosity; hook 1 is unchanged.
